parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what r.m.s. means for a sine wave - how is the peak value related to the 4.2 V value you are given?
Hint 2: Remember maximum power happens at the instant of peak voltage, so use $P = V^2/R$ with the peak value, not the r.m.s. value, and check your answer is near 0.046 W.
parts.proper_answer: Peak voltage $V_0 = \sqrt{2} \times V_{rms} = \sqrt{2} \times 4.2 = 5.9\text{ V}$. Maximum power $P_{max} = V_0^2/R = 5.9^2/760 = 0.046\text{ W} = 46\text{ mW}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link r.m.s. to peak voltage**
You are given the r.m.s. voltage, but maximum power needs the maximum voltage. For a sinusoid they are linked by a simple factor. Think of r.m.s. as a kind of average heating effect, which is smaller than the peak by $\sqrt{2}$:
$$V_0 = \sqrt{2} \times V_{rms}$$
So $$V_0 = \sqrt{2} \times 4.2 \approx 5.94\text{ V}$$

Step 2: **Calculate maximum power**
Power in a resistor at any instant is $P = V^2/R$. The largest $P$ uses the largest $V$, which is $V_0$:
$$P_{max} = \frac{V_0^2}{R} = \frac{(5.94)^2}{760}$$
$$P_{max} \approx 0.046\text{ W} = 46\text{ mW}$$
That is what you had to show. Note you must use peak, not r.m.s., because r.m.s. would give the mean power.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
key_concepts: power frequency is twice voltage frequency
P proportional to V squared is always positive
hints: Hint 1: Start by finding the period of the 50 kHz voltage from $T = 1/f$, then think why power goes up and down twice as fast as voltage.
Hint 2: Remember $P = V^2/R$ can never be negative, so what must the shape look like when $V$ swings negative?
Hint 3: Count how many times $P$ should hit zero and hit 46 mW between 0 and 40 microseconds if $P = 0$ at $t = 0$.
parts.proper_answer: Curve from 0 to 40 microseconds with peaks of 46 mW, $P \ge 0$ at all times with $P=0$ shape like rectified sine, and 4 full power cycles with zeros at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 microseconds.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the two periods**
Voltage frequency is $f = 50\text{ kHz} = 50 \times 10^3\text{ Hz}$.
$$T_V = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{50 \times 10^3} = 20 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s} = 20\ \mu\text{s}$$
Power depends on $V^2$, so negative voltage still gives positive power. Power is zero twice per voltage cycle and maximum twice per voltage cycle. So power frequency is $2f$ and:
$$T_P = \frac{T_V}{2} = 10\ \mu\text{s}$$

Step 2: **Get the shape right**
Because $P = V^2/R$, $P$ is always zero or positive. It looks like a sine wave sitting on the time axis, touching zero and rising to a peak. It is not a normal sine wave going below zero. Start at $P=0$ at $t=0$ as told.

Step 3: **Draw four cycles to 40 microseconds**
In $40\ \mu\text{s}$ you fit $40/10 = 4$ power cycles. Zeros at $t = 0, 10, 20, 30, 40\ \mu\text{s}$. Peaks halfway between zeros at $5, 15, 25, 35\ \mu\text{s}$ with height $46\text{ mW}$ from (a)(i).

parts.label: (a)(iii)
key_concepts: mean power as half maximum for sinusoidal squared variation
hints: Hint 1: Look at the symmetry of your $P$-$t$ graph - the area above the middle line cancels the area below it, so what must the average be?
parts.proper_answer: The $P$-$t$ curve is symmetrical about half the maximum, $46/2 = 23\text{ mW}$, so the mean power over a cycle is 23 mW.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use symmetry to find the mean**
Your power curve goes smoothly between 0 and $46\text{ mW}$. The shape spends as much time above the halfway line as below it. The halfway line is:
$$P_{mean} = \frac{46}{2} = 23\text{ mW}$$
The area under the curve above $23\text{ mW}$ exactly fills the missing area below it, so the average over time is $23\text{ mW}$. This is why r.m.s. voltage gives mean power.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Recall what a piezoelectric crystal does when you put an alternating p.d. across it - does it stay still?
Hint 2: Think about how a vibrating solid in contact with air can pass its motion on to the air molecules.
Hint 3: Compare the given 50 kHz frequency with the limit of human hearing near 20 kHz to name the type of wave.
parts.proper_answer: Alternating p.d. causes piezoelectric crystal to vibrate at 50 kHz. Crystal vibrations cause surrounding air molecules to vibrate, producing a longitudinal wave. Frequency 50 kHz > 20 kHz so ultrasound is emitted.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Crystal vibrates**
A piezoelectric crystal changes shape when a p.d. is applied. An alternating p.d. makes it repeatedly expand and contract, so it vibrates at the applied frequency of $50\text{ kHz}$.

Step 2: **Air is forced to vibrate**
The faces of the crystal push and pull on the surrounding air. This creates alternating compressions and rarefactions, so a progressive longitudinal sound wave travels out through the air.

Step 3: **Identify ultrasound**
Human hearing stops at about $20\text{ kHz}$. Here $f = 50\text{ kHz}$ is greater than that, so the wave is ultrasound, not audible sound.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think in reverse - if electricity can make the crystal move, what does the incoming sound wave hitting the second crystal make it do?
parts.proper_answer: Vibrating air forces second crystal to vibrate, and by the reverse piezoelectric effect an alternating e.m.f. is generated across it.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reverse effect generates e.m.f.**
The ultrasound pressure wave from the first crystal hits the second crystal and forces it to vibrate at the same $50\text{ kHz}$ frequency. A piezoelectric crystal under mechanical stress generates a p.d., so an alternating e.m.f. of the same frequency appears across the second crystal. It acts as a receiver.
